videos.title: Hairline: a free Claude Code skill that draws line animations that react to your mouse, plus 27 ready-made ones
videos.summary: Hairline (lucasmarkes/hairline, MIT, by Lucas Marques, about 1,000 GitHub stars as of Oct 7 2026) is two things. A library of 27 isometric line figures that answer the pointer (a vault you crack by turning its dial, a keyboard whose keys sink, a laptop whose lid follows your mouse), with no dependencies, for React 18+ or any web page. And hairline-create, a skill for coding agents: give it an idea and it offers two or three concepts, draws the one you pick to Hairline's ten rules on the same engine, checks it with a script and in a browser, and hands over one HTML file that opens from disk. Every figure on a page shares one animation loop, and a figure off screen does no work. Our test (Oct 7 2026, Claude Code with Opus 5, run hands-free so it picked the concept itself): "a coffee cup" gave three concepts and a carrier where the cup under your mouse rides up, passed its checks, one 37.7 KB file, in about 10 minutes. "A mailbox for a contact form" gave five mailboxes on a rail whose doors swing open and flags go up, in about 17 minutes. The library and the skill are free; Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan or API credits.

videos.title: 4 free Claude Code add-ons to switch on before you vibe code, and what two of them did in our tests
videos.summary: Four free add-ons for Claude Code. Superpowers (obra/superpowers, MIT, about 296,000 GitHub stars as of Oct 6 2026) stops Claude jumping straight into code: it asks what you're building, writes a plan you approve, then works through small tasks, tests first. It's in Anthropic's official plugin marketplace. The Karpathy-inspired CLAUDE.md (multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills, by Forrest Chang, about 217,000 stars) is one file with four rules derived from Andrej Karpathy's post on how AI models overcomplicate code: think before coding, simplicity first, surgical changes, goal-driven execution. In our small test (the same job, add discount codes to a made-up order module, 2 runs each, Claude Code on our PC) Claude added 64 and 77 lines and a new file both times without it, and 54 and 47 lines with no new file with it. The counts include tests, and every test passed. I Have ADHD (ayghri/i-have-adhd, MIT, about 54,000 stars; its README says no diagnosis is needed) stops Claude burying the answer: the next action first, no preamble, no recap. It stays off until you type /i-have-adhd and on until you say "stop adhd mode". Asked the same Netlify question once each, the answer went from 375 words to 184, with the same four fixes. Claude Octopus (nyldn/claude-octopus, MIT, about 4,000 stars) does nothing until you type /octo. Then it sends one task to other AI tools, like Codex or Copilot, and flags where they disagree. It uses those tools' own accounts or keys, or free local models through Ollama, and on Windows it needs Claude Code running inside WSL. The add-ons are free; Claude Code itself needs a paid Claude plan.

videos.title: VoiceStudio: a free, open-source voice cloner that runs on your own computer
videos.summary: The voice at the start of our video was made by VoiceStudio on our own desktop, on the processor alone, from one line of description (voice design: nobody recorded it). VoiceStudio is a free, open-source app (AGPL-3.0), built mostly by one developer, debpalash, with about 54,000 GitHub stars as of Oct 6 2026 and 3,124 commits since April. Give it 5 to 15 seconds of clean speech and it builds a voice you can reuse, then reads anything you type in it, turns a book into an audiobook or dubs a video into another language. It also goes the other way: talk, and it types for you. It has its own MCP server, so while the app is open Claude Code can make audio files in a voice you pick, with no API key and no account for VoiceStudio. What it makes carries an invisible AudioSeal watermark by default. Clone only your own voice, or one you have permission to use. Our test: their default engine, run from source on a Windows desktop (i7-10700F with an AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT, which PyTorch on Windows can't use, so processor only). It designed the voice in our video in 22 seconds and spoke a 6-second line in a cloned voice in 2 minutes 18. The voice model is k2-fsa/OmniVoice: the app is free to use for paid work, but that default model's weights are CC-BY-NC (non-commercial), so check the model's licence before you sell anything.

videos.title: Replica: a new Claude skill that reverse-engineers an app and rebuilds it as your own, and what our test found
videos.summary: Replica is 11 free Claude Code skills (MIT) by Jake Schincariol. Recon maps an app from its public pages and your own account (screens, flows, the data behind them); the others plan it, rebuild it screen by screen, add logins and payments, test it, score it against the original, read what its users hate in public reviews, rebrand it, write the launch page and deploy it. It rebuilds what an app does, never its code, logo or words, and its deploy step stops until the original's name and colours are gone. Our test, public pages only, on a popular scheduling app: in about 13 minutes Recon mapped 23 screens (13 of them inferred from help pages) and 10 flows, and estimated the full rebuild at about a quarter of a year, or a first slice in a weekend to a week. The Entrepreneur read 555 public reviews from 4 sources (App Store 500, Capterra 20, Hacker News 20, Trustpilot 15; G2 and Reddit couldn't be read) and ranked bugs and crashes first, then price and paywalls, with every quote linked. Good to know: the skills are free, but Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan, and the build and deploy steps use services you set up yourself (a database, payments, email, a host, a domain). The Python checks need Python 3.8 or newer. Start with one slice, the one flow people pay for. Features usually aren't protected the way code, text, images, logos and names are, but this isn't legal advice: run the trademark checks /replica-brand lists, read the terms of anything you used (including the original's, if you study it through your account), keep the original's name out of your app, ads and store listing, and talk to a lawyer before you sell if real money is involved. Reviews are research, never testimonials.

videos.title: Cloudflare's free security-audit skill: what it does, how to run it in 3 steps, and our test
videos.summary: Cloudflare open-sourced a free AI skill (MIT license) that hunts for security holes in your vibe-coded app and shows you how to fix them. Cloudflare built it to hunt holes in its own code. It maps your app, sends AI agents to hunt by area and attack type, and hands every flagged hole to a fresh agent whose job is to prove it wrong. False alarms are thrown out, holes it can prove come with a fix, and the rest go on a needs-checking list. The bigger system Cloudflare grew from it, with one more scanner feeding it, left 7,245 findings for its engineers across 145 repos. We tested it on Brew Notes, a tiny app we broke on purpose with 8 holes: in about 30 minutes it confirmed 6 of them, found a crash we didn't plant, threw out our cross-site scripting plant with a good reason (it could only hit your own account) and missed one (unlimited password guesses). Without "use subagents" in the request, our run did the whole audit alone, so step 3 includes it. Good to know: On Windows, use Command Prompt if PowerShell says scripts are disabled. If Claude Code was already open, restart it after installing. The skill reads your code: it doesn't touch your live site or edit your files. It uses a lot of your Claude usage: on our 3-file test app it took about 30 minutes, and about an hour with "use subagents" (same results there; the agent team is what makes the skeptic a separate, fresh agent), so start with the quick profile. Without a sandbox (for example on Windows) it can't run your app, so holes it can't prove go in NEEDS-VALIDATION.md; in our Windows test its two checker scripts also needed a workaround, which Claude handled. A quick run is partial: a clean report doesn't mean your app is safe, and Cloudflare says one run found about half of what repeat runs found.

videos.title: How graphics cards actually work (and why AI needs them)
videos.summary: Inside a graphics card are 2,048 tiny workers; the processor next to it has 8 big ones. A chatbot writes by guessing the next word, and every guess is math on numbers it learned in training: printed one per page, a big model's numbers would wrap around the Earth. On our own PC, the same chunk of AI math took the processor 10 seconds and the graphics card 1. Capp explains why with a classroom: 8 math professors (each juggling 16 problems) against a stadium of 2,048 students, a teacher calling one step to a whole row (that's lockstep), worksheets close by (the card's own 16 GB of memory), and the catch: when half a row needs a different step, they take turns. Then why AI's demand for chips and memory is a big part of why gaming cards cost more right now.

videos.title: Claude can animate now: 12 motion graphics, all code
videos.summary: 12 motion graphics, each one playing on its own slide: words that slam in on the beat, 608 dots that turn into Drip, one shape that becomes a dashboard, goo that bounces, a word tunnel, a coverflow, a chat that gets stamped, a bar chart race, a shelf where books vanish, a balance scale, a data center that draws itself, and a zoom from a chip to Manhattan. Claude Opus 5.5 built all of them in code in Claude Code, and each took a few rounds of fixes. The prompts below describe each motion so you can make your own.
videos.prompts_note: Prompts to try. They describe each motion (every state, the springs, the loop) the way we asked Claude for them; expect a few rounds of fixes, the way we needed them.

prompts.name: 01 Words → slam
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping motion graphic in code (HTML/SVG or Remotion, 30 fps, every frame a pure function of time). Dark background. Four words stacked: EVERY / FRAME / IS / CODE. They slam in one per beat, every 0.32 s: each word starts at 3x scale and a 12° tilt and springs to 1x with a little overshoot, with a quick orange glow on impact and a ring that pulses out from the centre. Last word orange, the rest cream. After the last word, the whole stack punches once and an orange underline sweeps in. Fade out in the last half second so it loops cleanly.

prompts.name: 02 Dots → Drip
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping particle animation in SVG. About 600 dots start scattered and drifting. Give every dot a target point on the outline of a simple character (a coffee cup with two dot eyes, a small mouth and wavy steam above it). From 0.45 s each dot springs to its target with a small random delay, so the character assembles in a wave; hold it breathing slightly; at 4.5 s every dot springs back to where it started. Use one spring function (damped, closed form) for every move. Dark background, cream dots, orange steam.

prompts.name: 03 Button → dashboard
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping 'one shape, never cut' animation. A single rounded rectangle changes state on springs, never swapping for a new element: a dot, then an orange 'Render ▶' button, a drawn cursor clicks it, it shrinks into a cream circle with a spinning loader ring, turns orange with a check mark drawing in, then grows into a white dashboard card with a number counting up to 12,480 and six bars growing in. Then it shrinks back to a dot and disappears. Name every state with its size, radius and colour, and animate position, size, corner radius and colour on springs.

prompts.name: 04 Blobs → bounce
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping SVG animation using a gooey filter (Gaussian blur plus a color matrix alpha threshold). Seven orange blobs orbit the centre, then spring inward and melt into one ball. The ball drops and bounces three or four times with decaying height, squashing on each landing and stretching as it rises, with a soft shadow that grows as it lands. At 4.5 s it splits back into the seven orbiting blobs. Light paper background, a small caption: SQUASH · STRETCH · SPRINGS.

prompts.name: 05 Words → tunnel
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second seamless loop: a z-tunnel. Streaks of light fly outward from the centre (speeds chosen so the loop is seamless), cream with every fifth one orange. Every 1.5 s a word flies from far away straight at the camera, scaling up exponentially and fading as it passes: SPRINGS, SEEK(t), BEATS, CODE. (last one orange). Dark background.

prompts.name: 06 Cards → coverflow
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping coverflow of 7 portrait cards (use your own screenshots or frames). The centre card faces the camera; the others rotate away in 3D (rotateY about 44°) and shrink as they move out. Every 6/7 s the row springs one card to the left, wrapping around so the loop is seamless. Light paper background, soft shadows, a small caption under it.

prompts.name: 07 Chat → stamp
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping chat animation. A user's orange bubble types out 'Is this book real?' next to a small avatar. Three typing dots pulse on the left, then a grey reply types out 'Yes! It's a bestseller.' A red rubber stamp slams down on top, reading IT ISN'T., starting at 2.5x scale and springing to 1x, while the whole card shakes briefly. Fade out and loop. Dark background, label it MADE-UP EXAMPLE.

prompts.name: 08 Bars → race
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping bar chart race with four racers (a round avatar or initial, a name, a bar and a number). Each racer's value moves between keyframes on springs, and the bars re-order smoothly by value (use a soft rank so they slide past each other instead of jumping). The leader gets a small '▲ 1ST' tag. At the end all bars shrink to zero and the loop restarts. Dark background, bars in four warm colours, label it ILLUSTRATION.

prompts.name: 09 Shelf → vanish
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping animation of a bookshelf. Fifteen book spines in warm colours drop onto the shelf one after another with a springy landing; a headline reads 15 BOOKS. Then ten of them vanish one by one, each tilting, lifting and breaking into a few flying specks, while the headline counts up 1 OF 15 GONE ... 10 OF 15 GONE in red. At the end the rest drop off the shelf and it loops.

prompts.name: 10 Scale → tilt
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping balance scale. A beam on a post with a pan hanging from each end (the pans stay level while the beam tilts). A character stands in each pan. Four small weights drop in one at a time, alternating sides; after each landing the beam springs to its new angle with an underdamped wobble. After the fourth weight it settles level and LEVEL. pops in. Then the weights lift away and it loops. Dark background, cream scale, orange pivot.

prompts.name: 11 Blueprint → live
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second looping 'blueprint comes alive' animation of a building in plan view on a faint grid. The outline draws itself with a stroke-dashoffset sweep. Then, in stages with a label popping in for each: racks light up in a diagonal wave and flicker (COMPUTE), dashed cable trays start flowing over each row (NETWORK), two power lines pulse into a substation box and battery cells glow (POWER), rooftop fans spin and a cool pipe and a hot pipe start flowing through the rows (COOLING). Fade out and loop. Label it ILLUSTRATION.

prompts.name: 12 Chip → city
prompts.prompt: Make a 6-second 'powers of ten' zoom in one continuous camera, with the world drawn in real metres. Start on one chip, then pull out to the rack it sits in (drawn as its 72 chips), the hall of racks, the building, the campus, and finally a city outline drawn to its real land area with the campus inside it. Animate the camera as a view width in metres, eased in log space on springs, and only draw each layer while it's big enough on screen to read. A label names each level. At the end, rewind fast back to the chip so it loops.

videos.title: Why doesn't AI just say "I don't know"?
videos.summary: In 2023 a lawyer asked ChatGPT if a court case it gave him was real. It said yes; it wasn't, and neither were at least five others. In 2025 two big newspapers printed a summer reading list made with AI: 10 of the 15 books don't exist. Why doesn't AI just say "I don't know"? It learns by predicting text, and a fact it saw once has no pattern to lean on. Then it gets graded like a multiple-choice test, and 9 of the 10 popular AI tests OpenAI's researchers checked give zero points for "I don't know", so guessing wins. Inside a Claude model, "I can't answer" is the default, and a familiar-feeling name can switch it off. What helps: tests that take points off for wrong guesses, telling the AI "I don't know" is allowed, and handing it the source.

videos.summary: Drip thought the model and the effort were the same knob. They're not: the model is which brain answers, and effort is how hard that same model works on this one job. Sonnet 5 used 99 tokens on low effort, 233 on medium, 314 on high and 525 on max, and got all 20 right. On low effort, Haiku 4.5 used 594, Sonnet 5 99 and Opus 5 71, so the smallest model used the most tokens. That's why the cheapest price per token wasn't the cheapest answer: per 1,000 answers (output only, September 2026 prices), Haiku 4.5 came to $2.97, Sonnet 5 $0.99 and Opus 5 $1.78. Capp's rule of thumb: fix depth with effort, fix know-how with a bigger model, judge by cost per finished task, and test it on your own task.

videos.title: How Claude actually works, one piece at a time
videos.summary: Drip's notes from Capp on how Claude writes: one piece at a time. It reads text in pieces called tokens, scores every possible next piece, picks one, adds it and repeats. It learned by reading a huge amount of text and practising that guess, and later training with feedback on its answers shaped it into a helpful assistant. On hard questions it can think before it answers, which uses more tokens. It only sees what's in its context window: up to 1,000,000 tokens on the biggest Claude models (as of September 2026). A new chat starts fresh unless memory is on, and with tools it can search the web, run code or use your apps (MCP is one way to plug tools in).
